name: Agomes
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 5 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Dempwolff, Otto. 1905. Beiträge zur Kenntnis der Sprachen von Deutsch-Neuguinea. Mittheilungen des Seminars für Orientalische Sprachen an der Königlichen Friedrich-Wilhelms-Universität zu Berlin VIII, Abt. 1: 182-254; section 'c) Agomes. (Hermit-Inseln.)', pp. 200-205.
catalog_locator: p. 201, opening note to the Agomes wordlist; transcription note p. 182
catalog_quote: Die Betonung findet fast ausnahmslos auf der letzten Silbe statt. Die Aussprache ist singend, klagend; nur die letzten Silben werden so gedehnt, die ersten oft verschluckt, so daß es schwer fällt, in langen Worten die erste Hälfte zu analysieren.

new_statements.quote: Die Betonung findet fast ausnahmslos auf der letzten Silbe statt. Die Aussprache ist singend, klagend; nur die letzten Silben werden so gedehnt, die ersten oft verschluckt, so daß es schwer fällt, in langen Worten die erste Hälfte zu analysieren.
new_statements.translation: Stress falls almost without exception on the last syllable. The pronunciation is sing-song, plaintive; only the final syllables are lengthened in this way, the first ones often swallowed, so that in long words it is difficult to analyse the first half.
new_statements.citation: Dempwolff, Otto. 1905. Beiträge zur Kenntnis der Sprachen von Deutsch-Neuguinea. Mittheilungen des Seminars für Orientalische Sprachen an der Königlichen Friedrich-Wilhelms-Universität zu Berlin VIII, Abt. 1: 182-254. Section I.c 'Agomes (Hermit-Inseln)', pp. 200-206.
new_statements.locator: p. 201 (PDF page 216 of the archive.org scan bub_gb_-ELWAAAAMAAJ), introductory note to the Agomes wordlist
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened extracted text of PDF page 216 carries the running head "Dempwolff: Beiträge zur Kenntnis der Sprachen von Deutsch-Neuguinea. 201" and the passage "Die Betonung findet fast ausnahmslos auf der letzten Silbe statt. Die Aussprache ist singend, klagend; nur die letzten Silben werden so gedehnt, die ersten oft verschluckt, so daß es schwer fällt, in langen Worten die erste Hälfte zu analysieren." (scanned reads "fallt"; the page scan shows "fällt", matching the report's quote exactly). The archive.org djvu scanned ( line 24550) has the same text. Section heading at the foot of printed p. 200 (PDF page 215, rendered and viewed) is "c) Agomes. (Hermit-Inseln.)", with the material dated Apr…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is on the final syllable, with only rare exceptions; the stressed final syllable is lengthened and initial syllables are reduced.
new_statements.exceptions: 'fast ausnahmslos' (almost without exception); no specific exceptions are listed. Dempwolff's wordlist prints acute accents on individual forms (e.g. tärü, märu, lätäröp, kähoö), which could be checked for the exceptions.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms elicited via Pidgin English from two adult male speakers (Daxda, c. 40, and Morad, c. 30) on the Hermit Islands, Nov-Dec 1902, plus a few words from Hellwig; a wordlist-with-notes, not a grammar. Schnee's independent 1901 wordlist (MSOS IV: 277-279) marks accents mostly on final syllables, consistent with this rule.
new_statements.identity_note: Dempwolff's 'Agomes (Hermit-Inseln)' and Schnee's 'Louf (Hermitsinseln)' are the same variety, Hermit [llf] = herm1237 (Glottolog hh.bib maps Agomes/Louf/Lup to llf); Luf is the main island of the Hermit group. The language is extinct or nearly so (Ross 1988 'nearing extinction'; Wikipedia: extinct early 1990s, replaced by Seimat [ssg]), so the 1901-1905 German wordlists are the only first-hand descriptions and no modern phonology can be expected.

sources.note: Comparative only: Hermit appears in the Admiralties sound-correspondence tables and genetic tree (pp. 317-320); no stress statement for Hermit or the Admiralties. Hermit data sourced from 'Smythe 1975 (Lup)'; Hermit listed as 'nearing extinction'.

sources.citation: Z'graggen, J. A. 1975. Comparative wordlists of the Admiralty Island languages, collected by W. E. Smythe. In R. Loving (ed.), Comparative wordlists I, 117-216. Workpapers in Papua New Guinea Languages 14. Ukarumpa: SIL.
sources.note: The only 20th-century primary data on Hermit ('Lup'); Smythe's wordlists may carry stress marks or an introductory note on transcription that would confirm or refine Dempwolff's final-stress rule. Ross 1988 uses it as his sole Hermit source.

sources.citation: Thilenius, Georg. 1903. Ethnographische Ergebnisse aus Melanesien, II: Die westlichen Inseln des Bismarck-Archipels. Nova Acta Academiae Caesareae Leopoldino-Carolinae 80(2). Halle: Karras. Appendix comparative wordlist (Taui, Agomes, Kaniet, Ninigo, Popolo), pp. 351ff.
sources.note: Nothing on Agomes stress. The one accent remark (p. 84 fn.) is about the Polynesian outlier Nuguria ('die Betonung von der samoanischen nicht abweicht'). The Agomes column of the appendix wordlist carries no stress marks or notes.

sources.citation: Schnee, Heinrich. 1901. Beitrag zur Kenntniss der Sprachen im Bismarck-Archipel. Mittheilungen des Seminars für Orientalische Sprachen IV(3): 229-279; section 'V. Sprache von Louf (Hermitsinseln)', pp. 277-279.
sources.note: No prose statement on stress; the only remark concerns consonant values (f between f and p, l between l and r, ch, b, uh). The 111-word list is printed with acute accents on vowels (anahák, talóf, hakúf, kuyún..), mostly on the final syllable, which is consistent with Dempwolff's rule but no rule is stated.
